html:
The first coins were struck in Lydia, a kingdom in western Anatolia, around 630 BCE: small lumps of electrum stamped with a lion's head. Coins of fixed weight, marked by the state, became a standard of value that spread across the world.

Electrum is a natural mix of gold and silver, washed down by the river that ran past the Lydian capital, Sardis. Before coins, people traded and paid in metal by weight, which meant weighing and testing every payment. A coin's stamp promised its weight and purity, so it could be counted instead.

Some of the earliest known coins were found buried under the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. Electrum was hard to value because the mix of gold and silver varied, so King Croesus (about 560 to 546 BCE) is credited with separating the metals and striking the first pure gold and silver coins. Croesus became a byword for wealth: "rich as Croesus".

The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Lydians were the first people to use gold and silver coins and the first to keep shops.

The idea spread fast:

  • The Greek cities of Ionia, and then mainland Greece, took it up. Aegina's turtle coins were among the first in Greece.
  • Cyrus the Great conquered Lydia in 546 BCE, and the Persian kings struck their own gold coins.

Coins seem to have been invented on their own in India too, with punch-marked coins, and in China, where bronze money was cast in the shape of tools.
sum: The first coins were struck in Lydia, a kingdom in western Anatolia, around 630 BCE: small lumps of electrum stamped with a lion's head. Coins of fixed weight, marked by the state, became a standard of value that spread across the world.
